newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - NatWest fails to make Barclays show hand.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - NatWest fails to make Barclays show hand.

text.p: National Westminster Bank Plc on Monday failed in an attempt to make British banking rival Barclays Plc come clean on whether it was plotting a takeover bid.
Britain's Takeover Panel, which polices City takeovers, rejected a call by NatWest for Barclays to clarify its position. NatWest had said the uncertainty was damaging its business.
"As far as we are concerned no party has incurred any obligation to say anything under the (takeover) code," Takeover Panel director general Alistair Defriez told Reuters.
He declined to comment further on the episode.
NatWest made the plea because it said the speculation, which first emerged just over a week ago, was damaging its business.
Its shares had risen by eight pence to 818.5 pence at 1030 GMT on renewed market speculation. At one stage in early trading the shares were up by 22.5 pence, far outstripping the rest of the sector.
Rumours began circulating when it emerged NatWest approached Abbey National to discuss a possible merger, but was rebuffed.

Recent problems at its investment banking arm have fuelled the speculation, particularly since the departure of NatWest Markets chief executive Martin Owen over the embarrassing 90 million pound ($150 million) options loss it discovered last February.

Barclays has consistently declined to comment on the speculation. Analysts said it was avoiding making a public statement as it does not wish to be held "offside" -- takeover jargon for stoking City rumours while at the same time declining official comment.

If a company makes a statement -- for example denying interest in another -- then the Takeover Panel will deem it unable to then make a bid for between three and 12 months, depending on the circumstances.
NatWest's frustration with Barclays' silence was understandable, banking sources said.

"I can understand why NatWest are concerned about it...it cannot be good for staff morale, to have this sort of speculation going on in the background," one banker, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
Analysts said Monday's rise in the share price was inevitably the result of speculation, and such rises would continue until it was resolved.
On Sunday NatWest was linked to yet another possible merger candidate, insurance and financial services giant Prudential Corp Plc.
The Pru is Britain's biggest fund manager with more than 90 billion pounds under management.
But the suggestion was played down by a banking analyst at one U.S. investment bank who said NatWest was not an obvious choice for a firm keen to increase its retail presence.
"I think the most likely result of this is that NatWest stays independent," he said, adding the bank would inevitably have to improve its performance.
And while many have been quick to say NatWest is clearly "in play", he dismissed the bank being a takeover target, saying any deal would have to be agreed between NatWest and a suitor.
For Prudential, other financial services groups with greater retail focus such as former or remaining building societies, were a more likely target.
But the firm, which has said it is interested in buying a branch network if the price is right and would improve returns, declined to comment.
"We never comment on media or market rumour," Prudential press officer Alison Burgess told Reuters.

NatWest had already declined to comment on the latest rumour and was also silent on newspaper reports that retiring Securities and Investments Board (SIB) chairman Sir Andrew Large would replace Owen as head of NatWest Markets.
The role is currently being filled by NatWest chief executive Derek Wanless until a replacement for Owen is found. ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
